The key to this mechanism is understanding what schools are *obtainable*.  Since most applicants prefer y, x, and w over z, z will likely be the easiest school to get into. However, my value for z is the highest at $72. I also have a relatively good priority at z (2nd).

My highest value is z at $72. I need to figure out if z is obtainable.  If it *isn't* obtainable, then my next best option is x at $67. If x isn't obtainable, then w at $58, and finally y at $51.

Given the general preference for y > x > w > z, schools y, x, and w will likely be very competitive.  My priority at y is 1, which is good, but many others also want y. My priority at x is 2, and at w is 1, but those schools are also popular. My priority at z is 2, but since most others dislike z, it's likely obtainable.

I will rank z first because of its high value and likely availability. I will then rank x second (value $67), w third (value $58), and y last (value $51). This strategy prioritizes maximizing my value, assuming z is obtainable. If z turns out *not* to be obtainable, I'll still get my highest ranked available school.
